+NPU-CI Contribution Guide
+=========================
+
+Last updated: 09/16/2026.
+
+This guide describes how to add CI test cases for verl on Huawei Ascend devices.
+
+The verl repository uses GitHub Actions as its CI platform and safeguards code quality and system stability through a layered testing architecture.
+The NPU-related workflows mainly include:
+
+* ``npu_unit_tests.yml``: runs unit tests.
+* Files ending with ``_ascend.yml``: run end-to-end tests or specialized tests for Ascend NPU.
+
+Adding New Test Cases
+-----------------------------------
+
+1. Datasets and Weights
+^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
+
+Weights and their absolute paths on the CI machines:
+
++---------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
+| Model Name                            | Absolute Path                                                                       |
++=======================================+=====================================================================================+
+| Qwen2.5-0.5B                          | ``${HOME}/.cache/modelscope/hub/models/Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B``                          |
++---------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
+| Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct                 | ``${HOME}/.cache/modelscope/hub/models/Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct``                 |
++---------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
+| Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct                 | ``${HOME}/.cache/modelscope/hub/models/Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct``                 |
++---------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
+| Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct                   | ``${HOME}/.cache/modelscope/hub/models/Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct``                   |
++---------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
+| Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct                | ``${HOME}/.cache/modelscope/hub/models/Qwen/Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct``                |
++---------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
+| Qwen3-0.6B                            | ``${HOME}/.cache/modelscope/hub/models/Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B``                            |
++---------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
+| Qwen3-8B                              | ``${HOME}/.cache/modelscope/hub/models/Qwen/Qwen3-8B``                              |
++---------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
+| Qwen3-8B-Base                         | ``${HOME}/.cache/modelscope/hub/models/Qwen/Qwen3-8B-Base``                         |
++---------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
+| Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507           | ``${HOME}/.cache/modelscope/hub/models/Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507``           |
++---------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
+| Qwen3-32B                             | ``${HOME}/.cache/modelscope/hub/models/Qwen/Qwen3-32B``                             |
++---------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
+| Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct                  | ``${HOME}/.cache/modelscope/hub/models/Qwen/Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct``                  |
++---------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
+| Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct                  | ``${HOME}/.cache/modelscope/hub/models/Qwen/Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct``                  |
++---------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
+| Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507                | ``${HOME}/.cache/modelscope/hub/models/Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507``                |
++---------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
+| Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct                  | ``${HOME}/.cache/modelscope/hub/models/Qwen/Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct``                  |
++---------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
+| Skywork-Reward-V2-Llama-3.2-1B        | ``${HOME}/.cache/modelscope/hub/models/Skywork/Skywork-Reward-V2-Llama-3.2-1B``     |
++---------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
+| Qwen3.5-2B                            | ``${HOME}/.cache/modelscope/hub/models/Qwen/Qwen3.5-2B``                            |
++---------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
+| Qwen3.5-35B-A3B                       | ``${HOME}/.cache/modelscope/hub/models/Qwen/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B``                       |
++---------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
+| Moonlight-16B-A3B-Instruct            | ``${HOME}/.cache/modelscope/hub/models/moonshotai/Moonlight-16B-A3B-Instruct``      |
++---------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
+| deepseek-coder-1.3b-instruct          | ``${HOME}/.cache/modelscope/hub/models/deepseek-ai/deepseek-coder-1.3b-instruct``   |
++---------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
+
+
+Datasets and their absolute paths on the CI machines:
+
++--------------+---------------------------------------------------+
+| Dataset Name | Absolute Path                                     |
++==============+===================================================+
+| gsm8k        | ``${HOME}/.cache/datasets/openai/gsm8k``          |
++--------------+---------------------------------------------------+
+| geo3k        | ``${HOME}/.cache/datasets/hiyouga/geometry3k``    |
++--------------+---------------------------------------------------+
+| dapo-math-17k| ``$HOME/.cache/datasets/dapo-math-17k.parquet``   |
++--------------+---------------------------------------------------+
+
+**Note**
+
+   ${HOME} is root.
+
+   In the GPU test cases the weights are located under the ``~/models/`` path. To adapt, you can use a symlink: ``ln -s /root/.cache/modelscope/hub/modelscope/hub/models ~/models``
+
+   The following are the raw datasets. Preprocess them as needed, for example:
+
+   ``python examples/data_preprocess/gsm8k_multiturn_sft.py --local_dataset_path ${HOME}/.cache/datasets/openai/gsm8k``
+
+
+1. Workflow YAML Template
+^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
+
+To add a new workflow, create a ``.github/workflows/your_yml_ascend.yml`` file using the following template as a reference.
+
+The main sections to modify include:
+
+* Workflow name (``name``)
+* Trigger conditions (``on``)
+* Runner environment (``runs-on``)
+* Container image (``container.image``)
+* Specific execution steps (``jobs.<job_id>.steps``)
+
+.. code-block:: yaml
+   :linenos:
+
+   name: your_yml_ascend  # Unique identifier of the workflow
+   # Trigger condition configuration
+   on:
+     push:
+       branches:
+         - main
+         - v0.*
+     pull_request:
+       branches:
+         - main
+       paths:
+         - ".github/workflows/your_yml_ascend.yml"  # Must include this workflow file path
+         - "path/to/affected_files"               # Related code paths to monitor
+
+   # Concurrency control strategy
+   concurrency:
+     group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
+     cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.ref != 'refs/heads/main' }}  # Only cancel in-progress jobs for non-main branches
+
+   permissions:
+     contents: read  # Least privilege principle
+
+   jobs:
+     your_job_name:  # Unique identifier of the job
+       if: github.repository_owner == 'verl-project'  # Only run on the main repository
+       runs-on: linux-aarch64-a2-4  # Hardware specification: a2 instance, 4-card NPU
+       timeout-minutes: 60          # Job timeout threshold (minutes)
+       container:
+         # Image to run; this example uses the vllm image
+         image: swr.ap-southeast-1.myhuaweicloud.com/base_image/ascend-ci/verl/verl:latest-cann9.0.0-torch_npu2.9.0post2-910b-ubuntu22.04-py3.11-vllm
+         options: >-
+           --shm-size 16g  # Shared memory configuration
+       env:
+         HF_ENDPOINT: "https://hf-mirror.com"
+         HF_HUB_ENABLE_HF_TRANSFER: "0"
+       steps:
+         - name: Check npu and CANN info
+           run: |
+             cat /usr/local/Ascend/ascend-toolkit/latest/"$(uname -i)"-linux/ascend_toolkit_install.info
+             npu-smi info
+         - name: Check initial pip list from image
+           run: pip list
+         - name: Checkout repository
+           uses: actions/checkout@v4
+           with:
+             fetch-depth: 0
+             clean: true
+         - name: Install dependencies
+           run: |
+             pip install --no-deps -e .
+         - name: Verify environment
+           run: pip list
+         # The following are the specific test steps (customize as needed)
+         - name: Preprocess dataset
+           run: python examples/data_preprocess/your_script.py --local_dataset_path ${HOME}/.cache/datasets/your_dataset
+         - name: Execute NPU test
+           run: |
+             ray stop --force
+             bash tests/special_npu/your_test_script.sh
+
+**Note**
+
+
+   Once new content is added under the ``${HOME}/.cache/`` folder, it will not be deleted when the CI run completes and the container is destroyed. Avoid adding content to this folder.
+
+
+3. Adding Unit Tests
+^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
+
+Steps:
+
+(1) Create or modify a unit test file (for example, ``test_xxx.py``) under the ``tests/`` directory.
+(2) If the test file path is not excluded by the ``--ignore-glob`` rules in ``npu_unit_tests.yml``, it will be executed automatically by the following command:
+
+   .. code-block:: yaml
+
+      pytest -s -x --ignore-glob="xxx" --ignore-glob="xxx" tests/
+
+(3) If the test path is within the ``--ignore-glob`` exclusion range, add a new step in ``npu_unit_tests.yml`` to explicitly run that test.
+(4) If you are adding a batch of related test cases, consider creating a dedicated workflow file to keep things clear.
+
+4. Adding End-to-End Test Scripts
+^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
+
+Steps:
+
+(1) Create the end-to-end test script under the ``tests/special_npu/`` directory.
+(2) Find the closest-matching workflow file ending with ``_ascend.yml`` under ``.github/workflows/`` and add a step in it to invoke the script.
+(3) If the test scenario is independent or relatively complex, consider creating a separate workflow file.
+
+5. Testing Strategy Recommendations
+^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
+
+* **Unit tests**: Cover core functions, classes, and methods to ensure logical correctness.
+* **Integration / end-to-end tests**: Cover typical training and inference pipelines to verify multi-module collaboration and hardware adaptation.
+* **Resource management**: Multiple jobs within one workflow run in parallel. Set reasonable timeouts to avoid jobs hanging for long periods, and keep each single job within 40 minutes.
+
+Following the steps above, you can systematically add NPU-related automated tests to the verl repository, ensuring that code changes are fully validated before being merged.

+# Model Evaluation
+
+Last updated: 07/14/2026.
+
+The steps are the same for different models; Qwen3-30B is used here as an example.
+
+We evaluate the model through AISBench, which supports evaluation with multiple inference backends such as vllm/sglang.
+
+## 1. Installation
+
+~~~bash
+git clone https://gitee.com/aisbench/benchmark.git
+cd benchmark
+pip install -e .
+~~~
+
+
+## 2. Download the Evaluation Dataset
+
+~~~bash
+cd path/to/benchmark/ais_bench/datasets
+wget https://opencompass.oss-cn-shanghai.aliyuncs.com/datasets/data/math.zip
+unzip math.zip
+rm math.zip
+~~~
+
+## 3. Weight Conversion
+
+verl now supports saving HF-format model weights directly using mbridge, so no conversion is needed.
+
+If the model weights are not in HF format, convert them to HF format first before evaluation.
+
+Refer to verl's native [conversion method](../../../../../docs/advance/checkpoint.rst).
+
+## 4. vLLM Inference Evaluation
+
+**Start the vllm_server service**
+
+Launch the inference server with the following command. Parameters to modify: model and tensor-parallel-size.
+
+model: the path to the converted HuggingFace model weights saved after training;
+
+tensor-parallel-size: the number of tensor-parallel replicas. TP is recommended to match the infer configuration used during training;
+
+data-parallel-size: the number of data-parallel replicas. DP is recommended to match the infer configuration used during training, default is 1;
+
+port: any free port can be set;
+
+~~~bash
+vllm serve /path/to/Qwen3-30B/ \
+       --served-model-name auto \
+       --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 \
+       --max-num-seqs 24 \
+       --max-model-len 22528 \
+       --max-num-batched-tokens 22528 \
+       --enforce-eager \
+       --trust-remote-code \
+       --distributed_executor_backend=mp \
+       --tensor-parallel-size 8 \
+       --data-parallel-size 1 \
+       --generation-config vllm \
+       --port 8080
+~~~
+
+**Modify the AISBench inference configuration and launch the vllm_client evaluation**
+
+Open the inference configuration file benchmark/ais_bench/benchmark/configs/models/vllm_api/vllm_api_stream_chat.py
+
+host_port must match the server's port; modify max_seq_len and max_out_len according to the model configuration.
+~~~bash
+from ais_bench.benchmark.models import VLLMCustomAPIChatStream
+from ais_bench.benchmark.utils.model_postprocessors import extract_non_reasoning_content
+
+models = [
+    dict(
+        attr="service",
+        type=VLLMCustomAPIChatStream,
+        abbr='vllm-api-stream-chat',
+        path="",
+        model="",
+        request_rate = 0,
+        retry = 2,
+        host_ip = "localhost",
+        host_port = 8080,
+        max_out_len = 512,
+        batch_size=1,
+        trust_remote_code=False,
+        generation_kwargs = dict(
+            temperature = 0.5,
+            top_k = 10,
+            top_p = 0.95,
+            seed = None,
+            repetition_penalty = 1.03,
+        ),
+        pred_postprocessor=dict(type=extract_non_reasoning_content)
+    )
+]
+~~~
+
+Open another terminal to run the evaluation, and launch the evaluation command:
+~~~bash
+    ais_bench --models vllm_api_stream_chat --datasets math500_gen_0_shot_cot_chat_prompt
+~~~
+## 5. SGLang Inference Evaluation
+Refer to the evaluation section in [Ascend SGLang Best Practices](../../model_support/examples/ascend_sglang_best_practices.rst).

+# Training Configuration Parameters and Metrics
+
+Last updated: 07/02/2026.
+
+For NPU-related features, visit: [NPU Advanced Features Guide](../../feature_support/npu_advance_features.md).
+
+verl manages all parameters through a hierarchical YAML configuration file. All involved configuration files are located under the `verl/trainer/config` directory.
+
+---
+
+## 1. Configuration Parameter Descriptions
+
+### 1.1 Common Configuration Parameters
+
+The following parameters exist and have the same meaning in both the FSDP and Megatron schemes.
+
+#### 1.1.1 Actor Optimizer Configuration
+
+| Parameter | Default | Description |
+|--------|--------|------|
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.optim.lr` | `1.0e-06` | Actor learning rate |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.optim.lr_warmup_steps_ratio` | `0.0` | Ratio of learning-rate warmup steps to total training steps |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.optim.total_training_steps` | `-1` | Total training steps; -1 means auto-computed |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.optim.weight_decay` | `0.01` | Weight decay, used to prevent model overfitting |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.optim.lr_warmup_steps` | `-1` | Learning-rate warmup steps; -1 means auto-computed from ratio |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.optim.betas` | `[0.9, 0.999]` | First- and second-order momentum coefficients of the Adam optimizer |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.optim.clip_grad` | `1.0` | Gradient clipping threshold |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.optim.override_optimizer_config` | `null` / `{}` | Override optimizer configuration (null for FSDP, {} for Megatron) |
+
+#### 1.1.2 Actor Policy Configuration
+
+| Parameter | Default | Description |
+|--------|--------|------|
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.strategy` | `fsdp` / `megatron` | Training strategy; fsdp for the FSDP scheme, megatron for the Megatron scheme |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.ppo_mini_batch_size` | `256` | Mini batch size for PPO training |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.ppo_micro_batch_size` | `null` | Micro batch size for PPO training |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.ppo_micro_batch_size_per_gpu` | `null` | PPO micro batch size per GPU |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.use_dynamic_bsz` | `false` | Whether to use dynamic batch size |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.ppo_max_token_len_per_gpu` | `16384` | PPO max token length per GPU |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.clip_ratio` | `0.2` | PPO clipping ratio, controls the policy update magnitude; typical range is [0.1, 0.3] |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.clip_ratio_low` | `0.2` | PPO lower-bound clipping ratio |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.clip_ratio_high` | `0.2` | PPO upper-bound clipping ratio |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.tau_pos` | `1.0` | tau parameter for positive-advantage clipping |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.tau_neg` | `1.05` | tau parameter for negative-advantage clipping |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.freeze_vision_tower` | `false` | Whether to freeze the vision tower (multimodal models) |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.clip_ratio_c` | `3.0` | Upper-bound constant for the clipping ratio |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.loss_agg_mode` | `token-mean` | Loss aggregation mode; options include token-mean, and so on |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.loss_scale_factor` | `null` | Loss scale factor |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.entropy_coeff` | `0` | Entropy regularization coefficient, controls the exploration level of the policy |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.calculate_entropy` | `false` | Whether to compute the policy entropy |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.use_kl_loss` | `false` | Whether to use KL divergence loss |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.use_prefix_grouper` | `false` | Whether to use the prefix grouper |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.use_torch_compile` | `true` | Whether to use torch.compile for acceleration |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.kl_loss_coef` | `0.001` | KL loss coefficient |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.kl_loss_type` | `low_var_kl` | KL loss type; options include low_var_kl, and so on |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.ppo_epochs` | `1` | Number of PPO update epochs |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.shuffle` | `false` | Whether to shuffle mini batches during training |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.data_loader_seed` | `42` | Data loader random seed |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.grad_clip` | `1.0` | Gradient clipping value |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.ulysses_sequence_parallel_size` | `1` | Ulysses sequence-parallel size |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.entropy_from_logits_with_chunking` | `false` | Whether to compute entropy from logits in a chunked manner |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.entropy_from_logits_chunk_size` | `2048` | Chunk size for entropy computation |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.entropy_checkpointing` | `false` | Whether to use gradient checkpointing for entropy computation |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.use_remove_padding` | references `model.use_remove_padding` | Whether to remove padding |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.calculate_sum_pi_squared` | `false` | Whether to compute the sum of squared policy probabilities |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.sum_pi_squared_checkpointing` | `false` | Whether to use gradient checkpointing for the sum-of-squared-probabilities computation |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.use_fused_kernels` | references `model.use_fused_kernels` | Whether to use fused kernels |
+
+#### 1.1.3 Policy Loss Configuration
+
+| Parameter | Default | Description |
+|--------|--------|------|
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.policy_loss.loss_mode` | `vanilla` | Policy loss mode; options include vanilla, clip_cov, kl_cov, dppo_tv, dppo_kl, gspo, sapo, geo_mean, cispo, gpg, bypass_mode, reinforce_is, and so on |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.policy_loss.clip_cov_ratio` | `0.0002` | Covariance ratio for clip_cov mode |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.policy_loss.clip_cov_lb` | `1.0` | Covariance lower bound for clip_cov mode |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.policy_loss.clip_cov_ub` | `5.0` | Covariance upper bound for clip_cov mode |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.policy_loss.kl_cov_ratio` | `0.0002` | Covariance ratio for kl_cov mode |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.actor.policy_loss.ppo_kl_coef` | `0.1` | PPO KL divergence coefficient |
+
+#### 1.1.4 Rollout Configuration
+
+| Parameter | Default | Description |
+|--------|--------|------|
+| `actor_rollout_ref.rollout.name` | `???` | Rollout engine name; must be specified by the user |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.rollout.mode` | `async` | Rollout mode; options include async, sync, and so on |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.rollout.nnodes` | `0` | Number of nodes used for rollout |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.rollout.n_gpus_per_node` | references `trainer.n_gpus_per_node` | Number of GPUs per node |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.rollout.temperature` | `1.0` | Sampling temperature, controls generation randomness |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.rollout.top_k` | `-1` | Top-K sampling parameter; -1 means disabled |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.rollout.top_p` | `1` | Top-P (nucleus) sampling parameter |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.rollout.prompt_length` | references `data.max_prompt_length` | Max prompt length |
+| `actor_rollout_ref.rollout.response_length` | references `data.max_response_length` | Max response length |

+## 2. Training Metric Descriptions
+
+The log metrics printed at each iteration of the reinforcement-learning algorithm are described below:
+
+### 2.1 Basic Training Metrics
+
+| Metric | Description |
+|------|------|
+| `training/global_step` | Current global training step |
+| `training/epoch` | Current training epoch |
+
+### 2.2 Actor Model Metrics
+
+| Metric | Description |
+|------|------|
+| `actor/pg_loss` | Policy gradient loss (PPO clip loss); the value of the policy gradient objective function based on the advantage function |
+| `actor/kl_loss` | KL divergence loss, measuring the deviation between the current policy and the reference policy (only printed when `use_kl_loss=True`) |
+| `actor/entropy` | Policy entropy, representing the randomness or exploration capability of the policy (only printed when `calculate_entropy=True` or `entropy_coeff!=0`) |
+| `actor/grad_norm` | Actor gradient norm (after clipping), representing the overall magnitude of parameter gradients during backpropagation |
+| `actor/lr` | Current Actor learning rate |
+| `actor/pg_clipfrac` | The fraction where the PPO clipping mechanism takes effect, reflecting the stability of the policy update magnitude |
+| `actor/ppo_kl` | Actual KL divergence of the PPO algorithm (current policy vs. old policy) |
+| `actor/pg_clipfrac_lower` | PPO lower-bound clipping ratio (some `loss_mode` have this metric) |
+| `actor/reward_kl_penalty` | KL penalty value, the mean KL between the current policy and the reference policy (only printed when `use_kl_in_reward=True`) |
+| `actor/reward_kl_penalty_coeff` | KL penalty coefficient beta (only printed when `use_kl_in_reward=True`) |
+| `actor/kl_coef` | KL loss coefficient (only printed when `use_kl_loss=True`) |
+
+### 2.3 Critic Model Metrics
+
+| Metric | Description |
+|------|------|
+| `critic/vf_loss` | Value-function loss |
+| `critic/vf_clipfrac` | The fraction where the Critic clipping mechanism takes effect, reflecting the stability of the value-function update magnitude |
+| `critic/vpred_mean` | Mean of predicted values |
+| `critic/grad_norm` | Critic gradient norm (after clipping) |
+| `critic/lr` | Current Critic learning rate |
+| `critic/vf_explained_var` | Value-function explained variance 1 - Var(returns-values)/Var(returns) (only printed when `use_critic=True`) |

+# Guide to Migrating Models to NPU
+
+Last updated: 05/14/2026
+
+This guide provides developers with complete practical experience for migrating models from GPU to NPU or independently adapting models on NPU, covering the full workflow: preparation, component integration, precision alignment, performance optimization, and long-run evaluation.
+
+## 1. Preparation
+
+Set up a base runtime environment that supports NPU execution, ensuring that the model loads normally and datasets can be read smoothly. This serves as the foundation for subsequent migration debugging and end-to-end business execution.
+
+
+### 1.1 Software/Hardware Environment and Dependency Configuration
+
+Refer to the official [Ascend Installation Guide](../../get_start/install_guidance.rst). If the versions of the inference engines (vllm, vllm_ascend) and training engines (Megatron, MindSpeed, transformers) that the model depends on differ from those in this tutorial, **use the versions actually adapted for the model**.
+
+### 1.2 Model Weights
+
+BF16 is the **default mixed-precision training data type** for training backends such as FSDP and Megatron in the VeRL framework. The Ascend NPU environment uniformly uses **BF16** as the baseline precision format, and weights need to be aligned and dequantized to BF16. Currently, A2 and A3 models **do not support FP8 precision training** and only support BF16 precision; the Ascend 950PR & 950DT series products will open up FP8 low-precision training capabilities in later versions.
+
+### 1.3 Data Preparation
+
+Following [Prepare Data for Post-Training](https://verl.readthedocs.io/en/latest/preparation/prepare_data.html), preprocess the dataset into parquet format: (1) ensure it contains the necessary fields for computing reinforcement-learning rewards; (2) reading is faster.
+
+## 2. Component Integration
+
+The VeRL framework adopts an architecture that decouples the inference engine, training engine, and weight-synchronization bridge (Checkpoint Engine), enabling deep separation of computation and data, which provides a flexible extension foundation for migrating and adapting models to Ascend NPU. When migrating and adapting models on NPU, it is recommended to first complete the individual adaptation and verification of each component — the inference engine, training engine, and Megatron-Bridge — and then advance to integrating and debugging the full VeRL pipeline once each component runs stably. For the specific feature support of different VeRL inference and training backends on Ascend NPU, refer to the [Ascend Backend Features Guide](../../feature_support/ascend_backend_features.md).
+
+### 2.1 Inference Engine Adaptation
+
+The VeRL inference engine adopts a layered architecture design. Through abstract interfaces and the factory pattern, it flexibly supports multiple mainstream inference backends such as vllm and sglang. During the migration and adaptation from GPU to NPU, the inference engine adaptation is recommended to follow this workflow:
+
+Before running the full VeRL pipeline on NPU, it is recommended to refer to the official model deployment tutorials of [vllm-ascend](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-ascend/tree/main/docs/source/tutorials/models) and [sglang](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/tree/main/docs/docs/basic_usage), and first get the **single-instance inference pipeline** working. Fully verify **basic inference functionality** such as model loading and initialization, normal tokenizer loading, single-turn/batch generation, stop-token termination, and long-context inference. After the underlying inference engine is stable and usable, integrate it into the VeRL training workflow.
+
+### 2.2 Training Engine Selection and Adaptation
+
+The VeRL mainline code abstracts the training engine as the `Engine` class, decoupling scheduling logic from the underlying training implementation through a standardized interface layer. This architectural design allows multiple training backends such as FSDP and Megatron to be flexibly integrated in a plug-and-play manner without modifying VeRL's core algorithms and scheduling logic, greatly reducing migration and adaptation costs.
+
+Currently, NPU has completed automatic device detection through the `is_npu_available` interface and automatically applies the corresponding NPU device adaptation patches. Now you only need to configure model_engine=fsdp/megatron to switch the training backend to FSDP or Megatron with one click. The system automatically loads the NPU adaptation logic for the corresponding backend without additional code modification. In VeRL, Ascend has adapted and optimized Megatron; for specific feature configuration, refer to the [verl-MindSpeed feature documentation](https://gitcode.com/Ascend/MindSpeed/blob/master/docs/en/user-guide/verl.md).
+
+### 2.3 Megatron-Bridge Adaptation
+
+Megatron-Bridge is mainly used in the VeRL framework to perform bidirectional conversion between the HuggingFace weights that the inference engine depends on and the mcore weights required by Megatron-Core. This feature can be enabled with the following configuration:
+
+```
+actor_rollout_ref.actor.megatron.use_mbridge=True
+```
+
+Megatron-Bridge has natively adapted a large number of mainstream model structures in the community. For the supported list, refer to [supported model](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Megatron-Bridge/blob/main/docs/models/README.md). When migrating and adapting models in the Ascend NPU environment, basic configuration can be completed based on existing community capabilities, but some model-specific structures and scenarios still require supplementary customized adaptation.
+
+Taking the DSA (DeepSeek Sparse Attention) sparse attention structure as an example, we introduce the customized adaptation method. Ascend MindSpeed supports DSA capability based on the absorption matrix. This feature requires splitting the original `linear_kv_up_proj` operator in Megatron into two independent operators: `linear_k_up_proj` and `linear_v_up_proj`. The weights required for the split need to be converted from the HuggingFace-format `self_attn.kv_b_proj.weight`, but the aforementioned native PR did not adapt this operator-splitting logic.
+
+Therefore, the relevant weight-conversion logic must be manually adapted to ensure the absorption matrix can be loaded and take effect normally. Only on the basis that the absorption matrix is available can the [sparse\_flash\_attention](https://gitcode.com/cann/ops-transformer/tree/master/attention/sparse_flash_attention) and [lightning\_indexer](https://gitcode.com/cann/ops-transformer/tree/master/attention/lightning_indexer) fusion operators be properly enabled. By introducing these two fusion operators, memory-access frequency can be greatly reduced, memory utilization optimized, and computation performance improved, ultimately improving the operational efficiency of large-model training and inference pipelines while reducing resource overhead.
+
+### 2.4 Full-Pipeline Integration
+
+After completing the inference-engine adaptation verification and training-engine adaptation development, refer to [Training Configuration Parameters and Metrics](parameter_and_metrics.md) to configure the relevant parameters of the inference engine and training engine according to actual business requirements, and complete the full VeRL pipeline integration to ensure the entire process runs stably.
+
+## 3. Precision Alignment
+
+Precision-issue localization for large-model reinforcement learning involves a complex pipeline with many influencing factors. Various precision issues are typically introduced by problems in the **training phase, inference phase, and training-inference consistency**. **Precision alignment** is the core key to ensuring that the training pipeline is reproducible and issues are debuggable.
+
+For precision alignment in the training and inference phases, refer to the official document: [Precision Alignment Guide](../precision_analysis/precision_alignment.md). Therefore, this section does not reiterate the basic phase-alignment workflow, but **focuses on training-inference consistency scenarios**, using the msprobe precision tool to carry out precision-alignment practice and issue localization and troubleshooting.
+
+### 3.1 Precision Monitoring Configuration
+
+After the full pipeline runs through, enable the precision monitoring parameter by setting `actor_rollout_ref.rollout.calculate_log_probs=True`. During training, focus on the following key metrics to judge training-inference consistency and model training stability:
+
+* **Training-inference consistency reference metrics**:
+  * `training/rollout_probs_diff_mean` (mean rollout probability difference). Under normal model convergence, this metric is recommended to stay within 0.01; if it consistently exceeds 0.01 or deviates significantly from the GPU baseline, a training-inference precision anomaly can be identified.
+  * `training/rollout_probs_diff_max` (max rollout probability difference)
+  * `training/rollout_actor_probs_pearson_corr` (Pearson correlation coefficient between rollout and actor probabilities)
+* **Model training stability metrics**:
+  * `actor/grad_norm`: monitor whether it shows an overall downward trend to judge whether the model is converging normally during training.
+
+In addition, configure the parameter `trainer.rollout_data_dir=./rollout_dump/` to save the intermediate Rollout results during training. By manually inspecting the exported Rollout data, you can verify whether model responses meet expectations and whether there is garbled or repeated output, which further confirms on the surface that the inference engine is adapted correctly.
+
+### 3.2 Collecting Precision Data
+
+When training/rollout_probs_diff_mean exceeds the reasonable threshold of 0.01, or deviates significantly from the GPU baseline, further collect data through the [msprobe](../../../en/dev_guide/precision_analysis/precision_debugger.md) precision tool for root-cause localization.
+
+### 3.3 Training-Inference Discrepancy Investigation and Alignment Practice
+
+After data collection is complete, first read the `construction.json` file for module-level data comparison. Ensure that the input data of `layer.0.input_layernorm` is completely consistent, then verify module by module and layer by layer to locate where the training and inference outputs first diverge.
+
+For large models, tiny numerical differences accumulate and amplify layer by layer, causing the results of training and inference (rollout) to diverge noticeably. It can even happen that the same token has output probabilities of 0 and 1 in training and inference respectively. Therefore, every discrepancy point must be aligned to be exactly equal as much as possible.
+
+After locating the discrepancy node, determining the adaptation and modification plan is also a key challenge. Because various open-source communities have multiple different implementations of related modules, to ensure the correctness of the model implementation logic, you should reference authoritative source code and technical reports from multiple sources and comprehensively determine the final alignment plan.
+
+#### 3.3.1 Common Training-Inference Inconsistencies
+
+In large-model reinforcement-learning practice, the typical root causes of training-inference inconsistency can be categorized into the following five classes:
+
+1. **Framework implementation inconsistencies**: caused by different implementation logic in the training and inference frameworks. Sometimes these are "semantically correct" (for example, different operator-splitting approaches that are mathematically equivalent), and sometimes "semantically incorrect" (for example, a missing scaling factor or an extra operation). Strict verification against source code and technical reports is required.
+2. **Precision-type differences**: for example, the training side uses BF16 throughout, while the inference side implicitly upcasts to FP32 for some sensitive operators such as normalization and then downcasts, causing truncation errors.
+3. **Hyperparameter inconsistencies**: for example, the hardcoded `eps` value in the LayerNorm module is not unified.
+4. **Parallelism strategies**: tensor parallelism during training vs. continuous batching during inference causes differences in floating-point accumulation order.
+5. **Randomness control**: implementation deviations of Dropout and sampling strategies between the training and inference phases.
+
+Below are typical real cases of training-inference inconsistency encountered during the GLM-5 model migration and adaptation.
+
+#### 3.3.2 Case 1: Framework Implementation Inconsistency of the FFN Activation Function
+
+Comparing from top to bottom, the output discrepancy was located at the MLP activation function of the first layer.
+
+The inference side already uses the NPU-optimized `npu_swiglu` fusion operator, but the training side still runs the native GLU small-operator implementation.
+
+* **Root cause**: Although the `swiglu` enable configuration has been added to the VeRL parameters, the Megatron-Bridge NPU adaptation PR did not explicitly configure `provider.bias_activation_fusion=True`, so the code did not enter the NPU fusion-operator branch.
+* **Fix**: Add the configuration items in Megatron-Bridge so the training side correctly invokes the fusion operator:
+  ```
+  +actor_rollout_ref.actor.megatron.override_transformer_config.swiglu=True \
+  +actor_rollout_ref.actor.megatron.override_transformer_config.use_fused_swiglu=True \
+  ```
+
+#### 3.3.3 Case 2: Precision and Hyperparameter Inconsistency of indexer_k_norm
+
+During strict alignment, a precision-type and hyperparameter inconsistency was found at `indexer_k_norm`:
+
+* **Precision difference**: the inference side upcasts to fp32 in LayerNorm with `F.layer_norm( x.float(), (self.dim,), self.weight, self.bias, self.eps).type_as(x)`, while the training-side Megatron implementation uses BF16. Tiny differences become non-negligible after accumulating across many layers.
+* **Fix**: Unify the training-side code to add the upcast/downcast operations.
+* **Hyperparameter difference**: on the GLM5 inference side, vllm inherits the DeepSeek-V3.2 logic, and the EPS value of `k_norm` is hardcoded to `1e-6`; whereas the training engine and the official technical report uniformly use `1e-5`.
+* **Fix**: Modify the inference-side EPS to `1e-5` to align with the training side.
+
+```
+self.k_norm=LayerNorm(self.head_dim,eps=1e-6 -> 1e-5)
+```
+
+#### 3.3.4 Case 3: Missing and Redundant Logic in the lightning_indexer Module
+
+Investigation found that the lightning_indexer module has inconsistent implementations between the training and inference sides, specifically:
+
+* **Missing (inference-side omission)**: the inference side is missing the scaling logic for `weights`. Referring to the standard implementations in the Megatron training side, slime, and transformers, all include this scaling, so it was added on the inference side to align the forward pass:
+
+```
+weights, _ = self.weights_proj(x)
++weights = weights * (self.n_head**-0.5) * (self.head_dim**-0.5)
+```
+
+* **Redundant (extra erroneous implementation on the training side)**: the training-side Megatron implementation has an extra `rotate_activation` (Hadamard transform). After consulting extensive materials, this operation was confirmed to be dedicated to quantization scenarios and is an erroneous implementation in BF16 format. Following [Transformer PR#45017](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/45017), this redundant logic was removed on the training side.
+
+```
+class DSAIndexer(MegatronModule):
+    def forward_with_scores(
+-		q = rotate_activation(q)
+-		k = rotate_activation(k)
+```
+
+### 3.4 General Routing Stability Solution for Large MoE Models
+
+In a typical RL training pipeline, efficient inference engines such as vLLM are usually used to sample data, and the sampled data is then fed into training frameworks such as Megatron for model training and optimization.
+
+For conventional dense models, implementation and environment differences between the inference and training frameworks only cause minor numerical deviations; but for **large MoE models**, this issue is drastically amplified. The core root cause lies in the MoE dynamic routing mechanism: tiny framework-implementation and runtime-environment differences can cause the same input token to be assigned to completely different expert combinations, thereby following entirely different computation paths.
+
+Such routing-decision inconsistencies may cause unstable RL training of MoE models. It makes the "experience" obtained from the inference phase completely different for the training phase, distorting the optimization signal and ultimately leading to catastrophic consequences.
+
+To solve this general problem, the industry has introduced the **Routing Replay** mechanism. Its core idea is to lock the expert routing paths of a specific phase, shielding routing decisions from the interference of minor perturbations, thereby ensuring the stability of model training. Currently, there are two mainstream variants, R2 and R3:
+
+* **(1) Vanilla Routing Replay (R2)**: (corresponds to `actor_rollout_ref.actor.megatron.router_replay.mode="R2"`, or `actor_rollout_ref.actor.veomni.router_replay.mode="R2"` for VeOmni)
+  
+  * **Mechanism**: In the gradient-update phase, it reproduces the expert paths computed by the training engine in the previous sampling phase.
+  * **Effect**: mainly mitigates the impact of **policy staleness** on routing. As the policy is updated, the routing computed in the current forward pass may differ from the routing when the old data was generated; R2 maintains the coherence of the optimization signal by replaying the old routing.
+* **(2) Rollout Routing Replay (R3)**: (corresponds to `actor_rollout_ref.actor.megatron.router_replay.mode="R3"`)
+  
+  * **Mechanism**: During sequence generation, it captures the routing distribution of the inference engine and replays it directly into the training engine.
+  * **Effect**: simultaneously addresses both **training-inference divergence** and **policy staleness**. It ensures that the expert paths used to compute the loss in the training phase are absolutely consistent with the expert paths used when the inference results were actually generated.
+
+Therefore, whether it is R2, which focuses on mitigating policy staleness, or R3, which achieves full-pipeline alignment, the Routing Replay mechanism effectively bridges the routing gap between the inference and training frameworks. In the training-inference consistency alignment of **large MoE models**, this mechanism has become a core means of ensuring precision alignment and training stability. Currently, mainstream large models such as DeepSeek-V3.2, GLM-5, and MiMo-V2 have all adopted the R3-mode Routing Replay technique.
+
+Therefore, for large MoE models, the R3 mode, which provides more thorough alignment, is generally recommended in actual configuration:
+
+```
+actor_rollout_ref.actor.megatron.router_replay.mode="R3" \
+actor_rollout_ref.rollout.enable_rollout_routing_replay=True \
+```
+
+For the VeOmni backend, use `actor_rollout_ref.actor.veomni.router_replay.mode="R3"` instead. The top-level `actor.router_replay` has been removed and is no longer effective.
+
+## 4. Performance Optimization
+
+When optimizing large-model RL (reinforcement learning) training performance on Ascend NPU, basic configuration tuning can first refer to the official document: [perf_tuning.rst](https://github.com/verl-project/verl/blob/04833f01/docs/perf/perf_tuning.rst). For more efficient optimization, it is recommended to follow the standardized workflow of **data collection -> bottleneck localization -> configuration tuning -> iterative verification**. This workflow can significantly improve the throughput of core phases such as Rollout, Reward, and Update, while effectively reducing resource idling and load imbalance. For the specific operations of performance analysis and tuning, strictly follow the official guides below:
+
+1. [Ascend Performance Analysis Guide](../performance/ascend_performance_analysis_guide.md)
+2. [Profiling Collection Guide](../performance/ascend_profiling.rst)
+
+### 4.1 Inference Performance Optimization
+
+The Rollout phase is the core inference stage of large-model RL training, and its inference time occupies the vast majority of the entire training pipeline. The following are common performance optimization methods for this phase:
+
+1. **Enable graph mode**: Graph mode compiles and optimizes the entire computation graph in advance, enabling deep optimizations such as operator fusion, memory reuse, and constant folding, which significantly improves execution efficiency.
+2. **CPU binding to accelerate operator dispatch**: CPU binding can improve operator-dispatch efficiency. Since vllm-ascend v0.18.0rc1, this capability is enabled by default on ARM-architecture Ascend servers.
+3. **Configure the HCCL communication algorithm to AIV mode**: Set the environment variable `HCCL_OP_EXPANSION_MODE` to `AIV` mode to specify that the orchestration and expansion logic of the communication algorithm runs on the Device-side Vector Core compute unit.
+4. **Enable async scheduling**: This eliminates the gap between two consecutive execute_model executions by the Worker, allowing the Worker to directly fetch the already-scheduled SchedulerOutput for model inference without blocking and waiting for scheduling.
+
+The corresponding configuration parameters are as follows:
+
+```
+# Enable graph mode
+actor_rollout_ref.rollout.enforce_eager=False
++actor_rollout_ref.rollout.engine_kwargs.vllm.compilation_config.cudagraph_mode="FULL_DECODE_ONLY"
++actor_rollout_ref.rollout.engine_kwargs.vllm.compilation_config.cudagraph_capture_sizes="[2, 4, 8, 16, 24, 32]"
+# CPU core binding
+++actor_rollout_ref.rollout.engine_kwargs.vllm.additional_config.enable_cpu_binding=True
+# Enable async scheduling
+++actor_rollout_ref.rollout.engine_kwargs.vllm.async_scheduling=True
+```
+
+### 4.2 Training Performance Optimization
+
+The Update phase of large-model RL training has characteristics such as large sequence-length differences and high memory consumption. In addition to basic operator fusion, it also requires combining sequence parallelism and memory-computation trade-off strategies to break through bottlenecks. Common training performance-optimization features can be enabled by referring to the [MindSpeed-verl documentation](https://gitcode.com/Ascend/MindSpeed/blob/master/docs/en/user-guide/verl.md). The core optimization methods include:
+
+1. **Operator fusion**: Enable fusion operators such as RoPE, SwiGLU, RMSNorm, and DSA. Operator fusion reduces computation overhead and memory usage, improving training efficiency.
+2. **Remove padding**: In RL training, Response lengths vary widely, and the traditional Padding strategy leads to a large amount of invalid computation. Enabling Remove padding packs multiple short sequences to fill the Tensor, greatly improving the utilization (MFU) of the NPU compute units.
+
+## 5. Evaluation and Verification
+
+After training is complete, evaluation and verification must be performed on the target dataset to ensure the model's business performance after migration meets the standard. The evaluation steps are the same for different models. The following uses GLM-5 as an example to detail the evaluation workflow (using the AISBenchmark tool, which supports evaluation with multiple inference backends such as vllm/sglang).
+
+The evaluation uses the math dataset aime2025 and the graduate-level professional science dataset gpqa, verifying that scores improve in the target direction while no catastrophic knowledge forgetting occurs in unrelated directions.
+
+### 5.1 Install aisbench
+
+```shell
+git clone https://gitee.com/aisbench/benchmark.git
+cd benchmark
+pip install -e .
+```
+
+### 5.2 Download the Evaluation Dataset
+
+```shell
+# Inside the Linux server, at the tool root path
+cd path/to/benchmark/ais_bench/datasets
+wget http://opencompass.oss-cn-shanghai.aliyuncs.com/datasets/data/aime2025.zip
+unzip aime2025.zip
+rm aime2025.zip
+```
+
+### 5.3 Modify the AISBench Configuration Code to Enable vllm/sglang Inference Evaluation
+
+Open the file benchmark/ais_bench/benchmark/configs/models/vllm_api/vllm_api_stream_chat.py. This is the inference evaluation configuration file. The output length `max_out_len` is recommended to match the training `max_response_len`.
+
+```shell
+from ais_bench.benchmark.models import VLLMCustomAPIChat
+from ais_bench.benchmark.utils.postprocess.model_postprocessors import extract_non_reasoning_content
+
+models = [
+    dict(
+        attr="service",
+        type=VLLMCustomAPIChat,
+        abbr='vllm-api-general-chat',
+        path="/path/to/GLM-5", # Change to the GLM-5 model path
+        model="GLM-5",
+	    stream=True,
+        request_rate = 0,
+	    use_timestamp=False,
+        max_seq_len=2048,
+        retry = 2,
+	    api_key="",
+        host_ip = "localhost", # IP of the inference service
+        host_port = 12890 , # Port of the inference service
+        max_out_len = 8192,  # Maximum output tokens length
+        batch_size=48, # Maximum inference concurrency
+        trust_remote_code=False,
+        generation_kwargs = dict(
+            temperature = 0,
+            seed = 1234,
+        ),
+        pred_postprocessor=dict(type=extract_non_reasoning_content)
+    )
+]
+```
+
+### 5.4 Launch the Multi-Node Inference Server
+
+Refer to the [vllm_ascend GLM5 Guide](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-ascend/blob/main/docs/source/tutorials/models/GLM5.md#multi-node-deployment) to launch the two-node A3 inference service. `host_port` should be consistent with the configuration in the previous section, and `max_model_len` should be set to the sum of `max_prompt_length` and `max_response` during training.
+
+### 5.5 Launch the vLLM Evaluation Task
+
+Run the following command to launch the online inference evaluation task, which invokes the deployed vLLM inference backend and loads the corresponding model configuration to complete the automated evaluation:
+
+```
+ais_bench --models vllm_api_stream_chat --datasets aime2025_gen_0_shot_chat_prompt
+```
+
+After training, the model's core capability metrics achieved stable improvement: the evaluation score on the AIME2025 math-reasoning dataset rose steadily, and continuous score gains were also achieved on the GPQA graduate-level professional science dataset, with no knowledge degradation or catastrophic forgetting. The training optimization effect met expectations.
+
+| Evaluation Dataset | GLM5-base | 10step | 15step | 40step | 50step |
+| ---------- | --------- | ------ | ------ | ------ | ------ |
+| aime2025   | 47.5      | 49.17  | 49.17  | 48.33  | 52.5   |
+| gpqa       | 64.65     | 68.81  | 68.43  | 69.07  | 71.21  |
+
+## 6. Summary
+
+This guide comprehensively covers the full workflow practice of migrating large models from GPU to Ascend NPU or independently adapting them on NPU. It is divided into five key phases: environment setup, component integration, precision alignment, performance optimization, and evaluation and verification, providing developers with actionable, reusable operation guides and issue-resolution solutions.
+
+In the preparation phase, focus on controlling environment-dependency versions, model-weight precision, and dataset format to lay the foundation for subsequent adaptation. In the component-integration phase, follow the principle of verifying single components first before full-pipeline integration, prioritizing the stable adaptation of the inference engine, training engine, and weight-conversion tool, and completing customized modifications for special model structures. Precision alignment is the core of migration and adaptation; focus on monitoring training-inference consistency metrics, and resolve common discrepancies such as framework implementation and precision types through module-by-module investigation. MoE models need the Routing Replay mechanism enabled to ensure training stability. Performance optimization should follow the standardized workflow, focusing on the core inference and training phases, and improving efficiency and reducing resource consumption through graph mode and operator fusion. Finally, standardized evaluation and verification ensures that the model's business performance meets the standard after migration, with no knowledge degradation.
+
+Overall, following the workflow in this guide can effectively reduce the cost of NPU migration and adaptation, avoid common pitfalls, and achieve stable, efficient operation of large models on Ascend NPU.

+# Ascend Performance Analysis Guide
+
+Last updated: 02/24/2026.
+
+## Background
+
+Following the release of DeepSeek-R1, large-model reinforcement learning (RL) training has attracted widespread attention. In the Ascend NPU environment, the verl framework has accumulated rich experience in performance tuning. This document systematically summarizes the methodology for performance data collection and analysis, aiming to help developers use the MindStudio toolchain more efficiently and achieve performance optimization in reinforcement learning scenarios.
+
+### Overview of the Reinforcement Learning Computation Flow
+
+1. **Rollout**: The policy (actor) model performs inference based on the input prompt sequence to generate a response (response sequence).
+2. **ref logprob**: Based on the prompt and the generated response, the reference model computes the ref logprob used for KL divergence computation.
+3. **logprob**: Based on the prompt and the generated response, the actor model computes the logprob used for importance sampling.
+4. **reward**: Based on the prompt and the generated response, the reward model evaluates the reward value R_N.
+5. **update**: Based on the computed R_N, ref logprob, and logprob, compute the optimization function and policy gradient, and update the actor model.
+
+![rl_data_stream](https://github.com/chengminhua/verl_data/raw/main/MindStudio_Insight_use/rl_data_stream.png)
+
+## Enabling the Profiling Tool
+
+### How to Enable
+

+## Performance Analysis Cases
+
+For detailed performance analysis, profiling must enable **level1**; otherwise, key operator information will be missing.
+
+### 1. Host Bound Diagnosis
+
+Host bound refers to the phenomenon where the total CPU task volume exceeds that of the NPU, resulting in idles (bubbles) during NPU execution. You can determine this by looking at the Host2Device synchronization lines: if the lines are all skewed, it proves that the set signal comes earlier than the wait signal, and the NPU executes as soon as it is ready, which is actually device bound:
+
+![host_bound_1](https://github.com/chengminhua/verl_data/raw/main/MindStudio_Insight_use/host_bound_1.png)
+
+If diagnosed as host bound, we can open the CPU side and find the dispatch time of each operator. Note that you need to find the cumulative value of all CPU time, not a single layer, because the first call takes a long time. For example, for GmmSwigluQuant in the figure below, the first call on the CPU takes 1ms, and each subsequent call only takes 200μs.
+
+![host_bound_2](https://github.com/chengminhua/verl_data/raw/main/MindStudio_Insight_use/host_bound_2.png)
+
+At this point, some operators are carrying a heavy load while others are dragging behind, and the latter outnumber the former. We prioritize **finding the top operators whose host time exceeds the device time; these are the operators dragging things behind**, and they can be handed over to the operator team for focused analysis.
+
+### 2. Network Architecture Rationality Analysis
+
+Sometimes the model network is not organized in the most efficient way, and this is very easy to identify in profiling. The analysis approach is introduced below with examples.
+
+Generally speaking, the large hot operators in an LLM are the matrix multiplication computations in Attention and FFN. Together, they can account for 70%+ of the computation time in prefill and 50%+ in decode. If the overall time proportion does not meet expectations, or new faces appear in the profiling, or there are too many concatenation-type operators, it is worth analyzing the model network to see whether the operators are being used incorrectly. Concatenation-type operators in particular are worth analyzing one by one.
+
+For concatenation-type operators like slice/split/concat and conversion operators like transpose/cast, their presence is often caused by the preceding and following operators not being directly compatible. If the preceding operator can directly perform tail-processing on the output, it can often save the startup overhead of one operator and one redundant read/write. However, such a change may not conform to the basic design principles of operators.
+
+As a positive example, suppose the output shape of a Matmul is [m, n0 + n1], and we then attach two slices, both taking this [m, n0 + n1] tensor as input and producing outputs of [m, n0] and [m, n1] respectively. The first optimization idea is to change the two slices into a single split, which roughly halves the time and allows the [m, n0 + n1] memory to be released earlier. A further optimization idea is to split the matrix multiplication weight from [k, n0 + n1] into [k, n0] and [k, n1], splitting the original matrix multiplication task into two (provided the combined time of the two is not much worse than before, and the core-splitting strategy does not cause issues), thereby completely eliminating the slice/split operation.
+
+![network_1](https://github.com/chengminhua/verl_data/raw/main/MindStudio_Insight_use/network_1.png)
+
+As a negative example, consider Rmsnorm(fp16)+Cast(fp16->fp32)+Matmul(fp32). Although Rmsnorm has fp16 inputs and outputs, internally it computes in fp32 to preserve the precision of accumulation. If the Cast is fused into Rmsnorm, the Rmsnorm—which already uses fp32 internally—can save the trailing fp32->fp16 cast, and combined with the eliminated Cast, we save two casts and avoid one precision loss. Although this seems to improve both precision and performance, an Rmsnorm with fp16 input and fp32 output violates the principle (the core input and output should be of the same data type). Unless we can frequently find such a structure in widely-used open-source models, proving its universality, the operator team will not allow such an operator.
+
+![network_2](https://github.com/chengminhua/verl_data/raw/main/MindStudio_Insight_use/network_2.png)
+
+### 3. Operator Performance Initial Diagnosis
+
+You need to use `"./ASCEND_PROFILER_OUTPUT/operator_details.csv"` for analysis to determine whether an operator has a performance issue.
+
+The Profiling tool computes the average busy time of these pipelines on different cores (xxx_time), divides it by the full kernel time of the slowest core (task_duration), and obtains the pipeline utilization (xxx_ratio). Although these pipelines depend on each other and the transfer-type pipelines compete for bandwidth, as long as the operator is properly designed, they can be mutually masked. Therefore, we can preliminarily consider that **when an operator's execution time is large enough, it should form a bound on one pipeline**, that is, the utilization should be high enough. Empirically, when a single operator takes 50μs, it can be considered that the operator should be on the bound pipeline, achieving 80%+ occupancy.
+
+Taking the figure below as an example, the first row is an FA operator and the second row is a Matmul operator. FA achieves 88.1% utilization on the vec pipeline, and the Matmul operator achieves 89.8% utilization on the mac pipeline. Their performance can be considered acceptable.
+
+![Operator%20performance](https://github.com/chengminhua/verl_data/raw/main/MindStudio_Insight_use/Operator%20performance.png)
+
+### 4. Affinity Shape Adjustment
+
+For a model, we cannot control the hyperparameters, but we can control factors such as concurrency, weight format, and splitting strategy to accommodate the operator and let it perform at its best. This section focuses on two aspects—operator transfer efficiency and load balancing—and discusses directions worth trying on the model side.
+
+#### 4.1 Transfer-Efficiency-Affinity Shape
+
+mte2 is a pipeline whose own efficiency is severely affected by shape. To ensure maximum transfer efficiency for mte2, at least one of the following two conditions must be met:
+
+**(1) The transferred matrix uses nz as format (optimal)
+(2) The tail axis of the transferred matrix is 512B-aligned and not an integer multiple of 16KB (approximately optimal)**
+
+For weight matrices, in the inference phase—especially decode—we usually satisfy (1), and in the training phase we usually satisfy (2). **If we cannot achieve (1), we should accommodate (2)**. Typical approaches include:
+
+1. If (1) is not achieved and the matrix's leading axis is affinity-friendly while the tail axis is not, transpose it.
+2. Adjust the TP splitting strategy to avoid an unfriendly tail axis.
+
+#### 4.2 Load-Balancing-Affinity Shape
+
+When the operator shape is small, due to operator semantics, we may not be able to utilize all cores, or even with all cores enabled, load balancing is poor. This subsection mainly analyzes the small shapes in the decode phase.
+
+First, we clarify how many cores the current NPU card has. If you are not sure, the numbers like 20 and 40 in the profiling output indicate 20 cores; otherwise, it is 24 cores. Here, 24 cores actually represents a group consisting of one cube and two vectors. We can consider it as one cube acting as the master core, with two vectors as slave cores. If an operator is a pure vector operator, the concept of groups no longer applies; the 40 or 48 vector cores act as master cores and directly take logical tasks independently.
+
+For vector operators in LLMs, one common core-splitting strategy is to split along the highest dimension, that is, the batch dimension, which is common in norm-type and dynamic-quantization-type operators that perform reduction on low dimensions (also called tail axis). The other is to flatten everything, allowing operators to be split very finely, such as elementwise operators. For the first type, we can focus on load balancing issues on the model side. For example, if we set a batch of 48 but the hardware has 40 vector cores, these 40 cores will loop twice, and in the second loop most cores will have nothing to do. This batch size can be considered unfriendly. If the batch is set to 64 or 80, performance is expected to be lossless. In the same situation, if it is a 48-core card, we can consider this a very friendly batch size.
+
+For cube-type operators, the common core-splitting strategy is to split M and N by base (the K axis is the accumulation axis, and splitting on it introduces determinism issues). The most common blocking is baseM=128, baseN=256. In the decode phase, the time can basically be considered as all spent transferring weights, because the activation M is extremely small, and the M direction most likely has only one block, so the right matrix only needs to be transferred once. Therefore, within the range of M≤128, we can freely increase M with basically no performance loss. If M exceeds 128, (128, 256] can be considered the next performance tier.
+Besides M, the tasks split on the N axis also affect operator affinity. Taking the MLA preprocessing in deepseekR1 as an example, it uses the same activation (shape [batch_size, 7168]) to do matrix multiplication with two weights (shapes [7168, 1536] and [7168, 576]). When batch_size cannot be made large, even if baseN is reduced to 128, the N axis still cannot use up all cores. So the time of these two matrix multiplications each is approximately equal to the time of multiplying the combined N axis of the weights (shape [7168, 2112]). If we only consider model competitiveness, we prefer to merge these two weights; otherwise, the bandwidth utilization of both small matrix multiplications will be very poor.
+
+For Attention operators, the common core-splitting strategy is q_seqlen, batch_size, and kv_headnum. In the incremental phase, q_seqlen is merged by MTP and GQA multiples, but usually still does not exceed 128, so a second task cannot be split out, and the parallelism is basically batch_size * kv_headnum.
+
+Overall, based on shape information and operator category, we can identify whether an operator has a load balancing issue, and therefore anticipate our splitting-strategy choices and the batch strategy for maximum throughput.

+Ascend Performance Tuning Guide
+====================================
+
+Last updated:  01/29/2026.
+
+Author:  `Xiaobo Hu <https://github.com/tardis-key>`_, `Haozhe Li <https://github.com/ZLiao097>`_
+
+The performance tuning methods introduced in `Perf Tuning <https://github.com/verl-project/verl/blob/main/docs/perf/perf_tuning.rst>`_ also apply to Ascend devices. This document focuses on several Ascend-specific tuning approaches, including fusion operator optimization, specific hardware configurations, and Ascend affinity features.
+
+Fusion Operators
+--------------------------
+
+List of Commonly Used Fusion Operators
+**********************************
+
+The optimization principle of fusion operators is to use mathematically equivalent substitutions to fuse the computation of multiple operators into a single operator, reducing redundant computation and the number of dispatches, thereby improving performance. Several typical NPU fusion operators are listed below; all of them have already been substituted for the Qwen2 and Qwen3 series models in npu_patch.py.
+
+For the full set of fusion operators currently used in verl, refer to `npu_patch.py <https://github.com/verl-project/verl/blob/main/verl/models/transformers/npu_patch.py>`_ 
+
+Matrix Computation-Communication operator fusion (MC2) 
+~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
+MC2 is a general term for a series of compute-communication fusion operators in CANN. These operators fuse the originally serial communication and computation operations together, optimizing performance through internal splitting and pipelined parallel execution.
+
+In vllm-ascend, you can specify the environment variable:
+
+.. code-block:: sh
+
+    export VLLM_ASCEND_ENABLE_MATMUL_ALLREDUCE=1
+
+This enables ``torch_npu.npu_mm_all_reduce_base`` in the ``RowParallelLinear`` of forward computation, merging the separate ``matmul`` and ``allreduce`` into a single fusion operator.
+
+`RotaryMul&RotaryMulGrad <https://www.hiascend.com/document/detail/en/Pytorch/latest/apiref/customapi/docs/en/custom_APIs/torch_npu/torch_npu-npu_rotary_mul.md>`_
+~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
+
+torch_npu interface:  ``torch_npu.npu_rotary_mul(x, r1, r2)``
+
+Parameter description: 
+
+- x: q, k. The shape requires 4-dimensional input, generally ``[B, N, S, D]`` or ``[B, S, N, D]`` or ``[S, B, N, D]``.
+
+- r1: cos value. The shape requires 4-dimensional input, generally ``[1, 1, S, D]`` or ``[1, S, 1, D]`` or ``[S, 1, 1, D]``.
+
+- r2: sin value. The shape requires 4-dimensional input, generally ``[1, 1, S, D]`` or ``[1, S, 1, D]`` or ``[S, 1, 1, D]``.
+
+`RmsNorm&RmsNormGrad <https://www.hiascend.com/document/detail/en/Pytorch/latest/apiref/customapi/docs/en/custom_APIs/torch_npu/(beta)torch_npu-npu_rms_norm.md>`_
+~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
+
+torch_npu interface:  ``torch_npu.npu_rms_norm(self, gamma, epsilon=1e-06) -> (Tensor, Tensor)`` 
+Parameter description: 
+
+- self: Tensor type, shape supports 1-8 dimensions.
+
+- gamma: Tensor type, usually the weight. The shape must match the last few dimensions of self.
+
+- epsilon: Float data type, used to prevent divide-by-zero errors.
+
+Output description:
+
+- The 1st output is a Tensor, the final output y of the formula.
+
+- The 2nd output is a Tensor, the intermediate result rstd of rms_norm, used for backward computation.
+
+`Swiglu <https://www.hiascend.com/document/detail/en/Pytorch/latest/apiref/customapi/docs/en/custom_APIs/torch_npu/(beta)torch_npu-npu_swiglu.md>`_
+~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
+
+torch_npu interface:  ``torch_npu.npu_swiglu(Tensor self, int dim=-1) -> (Tensor)`` 
+
+Parameter description: 
+
+- self: Tensor type, shape supports 1-8 dimensions.
+
+- dim: Int type, default is -1.
+
+Output description: 
+
+- The output is a Tensor, the final output y of the formula.
+
+`GroupMatMul <https://www.hiascend.com/document/detail/en/Pytorch/latest/apiref/customapi/docs/en/custom_APIs/torch_npu/torch_npu-npu_grouped_matmul.md>`_
+~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
+
+Function prototype:
+
+.. code:: python
+
+    npu_grouped_matmul(
+        x, 
+        weight, 
+        *, 
+        bias=None, 
+        scale=None, 
+        offset=None, 
+        antiquant_scale=None, 
+        antiquant_offset=None, 
+        per_token_scale=None, 
+        group_list=None, 
+        activation_input=None, 
+        activation_quant_scale=None, 
+        activation_quant_offset=None, 
+        split_item=0, group_type=None, 
+        group_list_type=0, 
+        act_type=0, 
+        output_dtype=None, 
+        tuning_config=None
+    ) -> List[Tensor]
+
+For detailed usage, refer to the linked title documentation.
+
+Using Fusion Operators with the FSDP Backend
+**********************************
+
+In ``verl/models/transformers/npu_patch.py``, the available fusion operators have already been substituted through patching. No additional operations are required; they are used by default.
+
+Using Fusion Operators with the Megatron Backend
+**********************************
+
+Megatron's fusion operators are integrated in MindSpeed and require specific parameters to enable: 
+
+1. **Flash Attention (must be enabled)**
+   ::
+
+       +actor_rollout_ref.actor.megatron.override_transformer_config.use_flash_attn=True
+
+2. **RotaryMul**
+   ::
+
+       +actor_rollout_ref.actor.megatron.override_transformer_config.apply_rope_fusion=True
+       +actor_rollout_ref.actor.megatron.override_transformer_config.use_fused_rotary_pos_emb=True
+
+3. **RMSNorm**
+   ::
+
+       +actor_rollout_ref.actor.megatron.override_transformer_config.use_fused_rmsnorm=True
+
+4. **GroupMatMul**
+   ::
+
+       +actor_rollout_ref.actor.megatron.override_transformer_config.moe_grouped_gemm=True
+
+5. **Swiglu**
+   ::
+
+       +actor_rollout_ref.actor.megatron.override_transformer_config.use_fused_swiglu=True
+
+6. **Permute/Unpermute**
+   ::
+
+       +actor_rollout_ref.actor.megatron.override_transformer_config.fused_permute_unpermute=True
+
+7. **MC2**
+   ::
+
+       +actor_rollout_ref.actor.megatron.override_transformer_config.use_ascend_mc2=True
+
+Ascend General Configuration
+--------------------------
+
+`Operator Dispatch <https://www.hiascend.com/document/detail/en/Pytorch/latest/apiref/ENV/docs/en/environment_variable_reference/TASK_QUEUE_ENABLE.md>`_
+************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************
+
+``TASK_QUEUE_ENABLE`` configures the optimization level of the task_queue operator dispatch queue, defaulting to Level 1. This configuration can reduce host dispatch time and can be used to alleviate the issue of excessive overall free time caused by dispatch.
+
+.. image :: https://github.com/verl-project/verl-data/blob/main/images/ascend/perf_tuning_task_queue.png
+    :width: 500px
+
+Level 0: Dispatch pipeline optimization is not enabled.
+
+Level 1: Splits operator dispatch tasks into two stages. Some tasks (mainly aclnn operator calls) are placed on the newly added secondary pipeline. The primary and secondary pipelines pass tasks to each other through the operator queue and run in parallel. Through partial masking, the overall dispatch time is reduced and end-to-end performance is improved.
+
+Level 2: Further balances the task load between the primary and secondary pipelines based on Level 1, mainly by migrating workspace-related tasks to the secondary pipeline. The masking effect is better and the performance gain is greater. This configuration takes effect only in binary scenarios; the recommended value is Level 2.
+
+`Communication Algorithm Orchestration Expansion <https://www.hiascend.com/document/detail/en/canncommercial/850/maintenref/envvar/envref_07_0096.html>`_
+************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************************
+Use the environment variable ``HCCL_OP_EXPANSION_MODE=AIV`` to configure the orchestration expansion location of the communication algorithm. Supported values are as follows: 
+
+- **AI_CPU:** The orchestration expansion location of the communication algorithm is the AI CPU on the Device side. The Device side automatically selects the corresponding scheduler based on the hardware model.
+
+- **AIV:** The orchestration expansion location of the communication algorithm is the Vector Core on the Device side, and execution is also on the Vector Core.
+
+- **HOST:** The orchestration expansion location of the communication algorithm is the Host-side CPU. The Device side automatically selects the corresponding scheduler based on the hardware model.
+
+- **HOST_TS:** The orchestration expansion location of the communication algorithm is the Host-side CPU. The Host dispatches tasks to the Device's Task Scheduler, and the Device's Task Scheduler performs task scheduling and execution.
+
+Inference Phase Tuning
+--------------------------
+
+Chunked Prefill in V1
+***************************
+
+The current version of vLLM has VLLM V1 enabled by default. Use the following configuration to enable Chunked Prefill:
+
+.. code-block:: sh
+
+    actor_rollout_ref.rollout.enable_chunked_prefill=True
+
+For the principle, refer to the `vLLM official documentation <https://docs.vllm.ai/en/v0.4.2/models/performance.html>`_.
+
+Graph Mode
+***************************
+
+Similar to CUDA, the NPU enables **ACL Graph** through the following configuration:
+
+.. code-block:: sh
+
+    actor_rollout_ref.rollout.enforce_eager=False
+
+.. note::
+    ACL Graph conflicts in principle with ``taskqueue Level 2``; **the two cannot be enabled at the same time**.
+
+Training Phase Tuning
+--------------------------
+
+FSDP
+**********************************
+
+.. csv-table::
+   :header: "FSDP", "Description"
+   :widths: 30, 60
+
+   "/","Shard optimizer only (Zero-1)"
+   SHARD_GRAD_OP,Shard gradients and optimizer (Zero-2)
+   "HYBRID_SHARD","Shard weights, gradients, and optimizer (Zero-3)"
+   "2D device_mesh+HYBRID_SHARD","Also known as HSDP (FSDP+DDP). For example, device_mesh=[2,8]: every 8 ranks form one FSDP group, with FSDP sharding inside the group. There are two groups that perform DDP between them, synchronizing gradients through allreduce."
+   "2D device_mesh+HYBRID_SHARD_ZERO2","The Zero-2 version of HSDP"
+   NO_SHARD,DDP
+
+FSDP does not support Zero-1. VeRL determines the device mesh value based on the number of cards and ``actor_rollout_ref.actor.fsdp_config.fsdp_size``, and uses Zero-3 for sharding by default. If the model is small (recommended to be smaller than 7B), you can set ``actor_rollout_ref.actor.fsdp_config.reshard_after_forward`` to ``True`` to use Zero-2 on FSDP/FSDP2 to optimize performance.
+
+Megatron
+**********************************
+
+When the model is large, using Megatron as the training backend allows for more flexible performance tuning.
+
+When DP parallelism cannot fit the model in memory, enable TP first to shard the model weights. If the model is still too large, enable PP for further sharding. If the sequence is too long, causing the activations to be too large, you can enable CP and SP for optimization. In MoE models, you can additionally enable EP to control expert sharding. If the experts are too small, to avoid sharding the weights too finely, you can enable ETP to avoid TP sharding in the MoE part and instead distribute multiple complete experts across DP and TP.
+
+TP, PP, EP, and ETP are used in the same way as Megatron. The way to enable CP and SP on the NPU is as follows: 
+
+- SP: ``Sequence Parallel`` further improves computation efficiency on top of Tensor Parallel. It is a parallel computation method that shards the input data along the sequence dimension. On the NPU, SP is invoked through MindSpeed:
+  ::
+
+      actor_rollout_ref.actor.megatron.override_transformer_config.sequence_parallel=True
+
+- CP: ``Context Parallel`` is a method for parallel processing of neural network activations across multiple GPUs/NPUs. It is implemented by partitioning the input tensor along the sequence dimension. On the NPU, CP is invoked through MindSpeed (the two parameters must be added together):
+  ::
+
+      actor_rollout_ref.actor.megatron.context_parallel_size
+      actor_rollout_ref.actor.megatron.override_transformer_config.context_parallel_size
+
+Megatron-distributed optimizer
+**********************************
+
+When facing larger-sized models, it is usually necessary to shard the optimizer to each card within a DP domain to save memory. To enable the distributed optimizer on the NPU under the Megatron backend:
+
+::
+
+    +actor_rollout_ref.actor.megatron.override_transformer_config.use_distributed_optimizer=True
